title: The FAO Says Global Cereal Output Will Shrink for the First Time in Years. Two Crises Are Converging.
excerpt: Wheat prices are up for a fourth straight month, fertiliser costs are spiking from the Hormuz closure, and the strongest El Niño on record is forming. The impact on Indian kitchens is coming.
body:
The United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization's benchmark index for world food prices slipped just 0.2 per cent in May from a revised April level — and stayed near its highest point since January 2023. The headline number masks something more urgent. Cereal prices climbed 2.6 per cent in a single month. Wheat rose for a fourth straight month. Rice edged higher on weather worries and rising energy costs. Sugar jumped 7.5 per cent.

Two forces that rarely hit at the same time are now converging. One is man-made: the near-total closure of the Strait of Hormuz has sent global fertiliser prices surging, because the Gulf accounts for a disproportionate share of the world's nitrogen and phosphate exports. The other is natural: the World Meteorological Organisation said this week that one of the strongest El Niños on record is widely expected to develop in the second half of 2026, bringing drought to India, Southeast Asia and Australia.

## Cereal production to shrink for the first time in years

The FAO's separate supply report, released the same day, forecast that world cereal production would fall 2 per cent in the 2026-27 season to 2.98 billion tonnes. Production of wheat, rice and maize is all expected to decline. For wheat, the percentage drop is the largest among major cereals.

That matters for India more than most. The country is the world's second-largest wheat producer and its largest rice exporter. A bad monsoon — and the India Meteorological Department forecasts the worst in 11 years — could force New Delhi to restrict exports again, as it did in 2022 and 2023. That would ripple through global markets.

## Farmers face an impossible choice

FAO Chief Economist Máximo Torero has been blunt. If the Iran conflict stretches on and fertiliser costs stay elevated while commodity margins remain thin, farmers will be forced to choose: farm the same acreage with fewer inputs, plant less land, or switch to less fertiliser-intensive crops. All three options lead to lower yields.

The delayed nature of the shock makes it politically dangerous. Many farmers secured fertiliser supplies before the conflict escalated, so current harvests may look normal. The full impact on yields and production will materialise in the next planting season — by which time the policy window to act will have narrowed.

Vegetable oil prices fell 4.6 per cent from last month, their first monthly decline this year, as lower palm and soy oil prices outweighed gains in rapeseed and sunflower oil. But they remain more than 20 per cent above last year's levels, driven by elevated energy costs that have boosted demand for biofuels made from oil-rich plants.

## What NRIs should watch

For the Indian diaspora, three things matter. First, food inflation at home: staple prices in India are already sensitive to monsoon performance, and a weak monsoon combined with global cereal tightening could push prices higher just as the RBI is trying to hold rates steady. Second, remittance purchasing power: every rupee sent home buys less if food prices spike. Third, the political fallout: food inflation is the single most potent political variable in Indian elections.

The OECD projects that average global agricultural commodity prices could rise 4.5 per cent in 2026 and 8.3 per cent in 2027 under its oil-shock scenario. Wheat, the most fertiliser-intensive crop, is expected to see the strongest increases. UBS analysts warn that a transition from neutral to strong El Niño could push global food commodity prices up by as much as 9 per cent over two years.

China adds another variable. Heavy rains during the recent wheat harvest damaged up to 10 million tonnes of grain in Henan and Hubei provinces — the country's largest producing regions. Analysts estimate 4.8 to 10 million tonnes of wheat sprouted and became unsuitable for milling. Even a modest increase in Chinese imports would push global prices higher still.

For now, the FAO's headline number still looks manageable. It is the direction that should concern policymakers — and the families who depend on stable food prices to make ends meet.
